title: Effective code reviews
description: Learn how to run code reviews that improve code quality, share knowledge, and strengthen your team without becoming a bottleneck.

data.text: Code reviews are one of the most powerful tools a senior engineer has. Done well, they catch bugs early, spread knowledge across the team, and raise the overall quality of the codebase. Done poorly, they slow down delivery, frustrate authors, and create unnecessary tension. This lesson focuses on making your reviews both effective and respectful.

As a senior engineer, your reviews set the tone for the entire team. Junior engineers watch how you review code and model their behavior after yours. That means your feedback should be clear, constructive, and consistent.
The goals of a code review

A good code review serves several purposes at once. It checks correctness, but it also shares context, improves readability, and helps the author grow. If you focus only on catching mistakes, you miss the bigger picture.

items: Correctness: Does the code do what it claims to do?
Maintainability: Will someone else understand this in six months?
Security: Are there obvious vulnerabilities or unsafe patterns?
Consistency: Does the change follow the project's existing patterns?
Learning: Does the review help the author improve their skills?

data.text: Giving feedback that people can act on

The way you phrase feedback matters more than the feedback itself. Vague comments like 'this is wrong' or 'refactor this' leave the author guessing. Specific, actionable comments lead to faster improvements and less frustration.

data.title: Weak feedback vs. strong feedback
data.code:
Weak: "This function is messy."
Strong: "This function handles parsing, validation, and database storage all at once. Consider splitting it into three smaller functions so each piece can be tested and reviewed independently."

data.text: Notice the difference. The strong version explains what is wrong, why it matters, and how to fix it. The author can act on it immediately without a follow-up meeting.
Not all comments carry the same weight. If you mark everything as critical, nothing is critical. Use labels or simple prefixes to show the priority of each comment.

items: [suggestion] A possible improvement but not required.
[question] I need more context to understand the approach.
[nit] A very small style preference; feel free to ignore.

data.text: Readability is not about style nitpicking. It is about whether another engineer can read the code and understand the intent quickly. Good naming, clear structure, and helpful comments all contribute to readability.

data.title: The six-month test
data.text: Ask yourself: if you read this code six months from now, with no memory of writing it, would you understand what it does? If the answer is no, ask for a rename, a helper function, or a brief comment.

data.title: Key takeaways
data.text: Great code reviews are a conversation, not an inspection. Focus on correctness, maintainability, and growth. Be specific with feedback, label its priority, and treat readability as a team responsibility, not a personal preference.
